metas.name: Alberta  - Central rumble strips
metas.note:
Within the Prairies, rumble strips on the centre line are only found in Alberta.

Note: Rumble strips on the outer lines can also be found in other provinces.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Alberta  - Extreme Southwest
metas.note: In the extreme Southwest of Alberta you will find slightly rolling, grassy fields with the Southern Rockies visible to the West.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Alberta  - Generic guardrail
metas.note: Alberta tends to use more generic guardrails than any other Prairies province. Sask and Manitoba have way less guardrails in general and those are often of an unconventional type.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Alberta  - Horizontal sticker
metas.note: Even though pole stickers are not the most reliable in the Prairies, horizontal metal stickers are common in Alberta. They are usually grey and can be either blank or have small numbers on them. Yellow variants exist too.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Alberta  - Isolated hills
metas.note:
From certain roads in Far Southern Alberta isolated hills can be seen over the border in Montana.

Note: They are best visible from Provincial Highways 501 (Gen 4), 500 (Gen 2) and 880 (Gen 2).
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Alberta  - Missing insulator poletop
metas.note:
Alberta has a poletop that is similar to the one found in Manitoba, but with a missing insulator on the bottom crossbar.

Note: The poletop is found in abundance around Edmonton.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Alberta  - Northern > poletop
metas.note:
A very distinct ">" shaped poletop can be found on the roads of Northern Alberta.

Note: It is especially common on the MacKenzie Highway (Hwy 35) between High Level and Warrenzie, as well as West of High Level on Hwy 58.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Alberta  - Peace River street sign
metas.note:
While most rural street signs in Alberta are blue, green signs can be found concentrated around the Peace River Area in the Northwest.

Note: In the rest of the Prairies, green is the standard rural street sign colour. Larger cities in Alberta often use green as well.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Alberta  - Standard Canadian lamp
metas.note:
Lamps in Alberta follow the standard Canadian design: no curve, no support bar.

To differentiate from other Prairies:

  • Sask lamps often have a curve and a support bar
  • Manitoba can use the same type, or an excessively long, supported lamp arm.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Alberta  - Standard poletop
metas.note: The standard Alberta poletop looks fairly generic: it has a medium-lenght crossbar with 3 vertical insulators each connected to its own wire.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Atlantic Canada  - Blue house number
metas.note:
Rural house numbers in Nova Scotia tend to be blue with white lettering.

Note: This style is also common in New Brunswick and PEI, only less consistently. Make sure to look for other clues first!
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: Atlantic Canada  - Clapboard architecture
metas.note:
While houses made of white siding wood are generally common throughout rural Canada, with some practice the iconic Atlantic Coast clapboard houses can be recognised. Influenced by British and New England architecture, these houses feature steep dark grey gable roofs, multiple stories, simple symmetrical facades and often an elaborate entryway.

Note: This style gets more common the closer you get to the Atlantic coastline. Look for the coastal village setting!
metas.footer: meta from: original research, based on "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: Atlantic Canada  - Colourful houses
metas.note: Aside from the white wooden houses, Eastern Canada also has a lot of colourful houses. They are especially common in fishing villages in the Maritimes, in coastal Québec as well as some bigger towns such as downtown St John's (NL) and Lunenburg (NS).
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: Atlantic Canada  - Square lamp
metas.note:
Square lamp heads are common in both New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island. To differentiate, you can look at the lamp arm: NB mostly uses long, straight ones while NS prefers short and curved. PEI's lamps are usually similar to the ones in Nova Scotia, although I have also seen the New Brunswick style there.

Note: Don't rely on the blue bumps on the top of the lamps being only in NS as NB also has them!
metas.footer: meta from: original find

metas.name: British Columbia  - 2+1 poletop
metas.note:
Poletops with asymmetrical insulators, arranged in a 2+1 pattern are common in British Columbia.

Note: They don't alternate like the ones in Saskatchewan.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: British Columbia  - Darker poles
metas.note: Poles in Western Canada - especially in BC - tend to be darker and have fewer knots than poles in the East. In BC, it is common to find poles with a reddish tint.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: British Columbia  - Double crossbeam
metas.note: Double crossbeams can often be found on utility poles in British Columbia.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: British Columbia  - Fake Ontario poletop
metas.note:
Occasionally, you might find poletops in BC that resemble the classic Ontario poletops.

To avoid the bait, here are some details to look for:

  • ON never uses generic mushroom insulators on a V-poletop
  • completely flat or strangely long "U" attachments are BC only
  • BC's insulators usually have longer and thinner ribs than ON.

...but the best is just to look at the landscape first.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: British Columbia  - Flat land
metas.note:
British Columbia has 3 main areas with flat land:

  • in the Southwestern lowlands nearby Vancouver (Fraser River delta)
  • in the Centre, nearby Prince George (Fraser and Nachako River valleys)
  • in the Northeast, from Fort St John and northwards (Peace River area).
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: British Columbia  - Hydro box
metas.note:
In British Columbia, large green electric boxes often feature the name of the local electricity distributor, "BC Hydro", or simply "Hydro".

Note: Unfortunately, large green boxes are quite rare in BC. (You might find 1 or 2 per town.)
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: British Columbia  - Longer secondary crossarm
metas.note: In British Columbia, secondary crossarms on utility poles are usually longer than the top ones.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: British Columbia  - Metal circles
metas.note: BC would often have 1 to 5 small metal circles at the lower part of her utility poles.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: British Columbia  - Metal flare
metas.note: Metal flares at the bottom of the utility pole are typical for British Columbia.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: British Columbia  - Metal pole rectangle
metas.note: Small yellow or grey metal rectangles are found on most utility poles in BC.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: British Columbia  - Northeastern landscape
metas.note: The Northeastern region of British Columbia is known for its rolling hills and vast boreal forests with white aspen trees. Aside for a short section of the BC-97 going through the Northern Rockies, there is no coverage with tall mountains here.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: British Columbia  - Northwestern landscape
metas.note:
Northwestern British Columbia can be recongised by its large, often snow-capped mountains, tall but thin evergreens, low green bushes, boreal mosses and flowers. The roads here still have Gen 2 coverage, adding to the remote, Alpine vibes.

Note: The extreme Northwest near the Yukon border has ominously gray, cloudy weather.
metas.footer: meta from: original find.

metas.name: British Columbia  - Redcedar needles
metas.note:
On Vancouver Island and the nearby humid coastal areas of Southwestern British Columbia, you can often see a reddish carpet of fallen pine needles covering the sides of the road. This is caused by the Western redcedar shedding its needles, with some contribution from Douglas firs.

Note: Redcedar needles can also be found in the temperate rainforest areas of Oregon and Washington in the US. Small, isolated pockets might also occur further inland in BC, but they are less obvious.
metas.footer: meta from: rachek (irl find)

metas.name: British Columbia  - Standard poletop
metas.note:
The most common poletop in British Columbia is a simple T-poletop with 3 (usually white) mushroom insulators. The middle one is mounted higher than the other 2.

Note: This poletop also exists with large UFO-shaped insulators in BC.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: British Columbia  - Stoplights
metas.note:
Stoplights in British Columbia are always vertical and yellow. The middle part can be yellow (eg. Vancouver City, Kamloops) or black.

Note: Middle part colours can be quite inconsistent, even within the same town.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: British Columbia  - Vancouver Island vibes
metas.note:
Parts of Vancouver Island is covered by a temperate rainforest. Trees are even taller and denser here than in most other parts of the province.

Note: Gen 3 is still quite common on Vancouver Island.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: British Columbia  - Yellow fire hydrants
metas.note:
Within British Columbia, you can use fire hydrant body colours for further regionguessing. Yellow body hydrants are found in the Central regions of the province, from the Peace River area through the Okanagan valley, down to the US border.

The peripheries of the province use red body hydrants.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: British Columbia / Alberta  - Rockies
metas.note: To distinguish the Canadian Rockies from the Coast Mountains and other ranges in Western Canada, you can look for sharp, treeless mountaintops and exposed rocks of a lighter colour.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: British Columbia / Alberta  - Yellow curbs
metas.note:
Yellow curbs can often be seen in British Columbia and Alberta.

Note: Other provinces can also have them, so only use this meta if you can't find anything better.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: British Columbia / Québec  - "L" poletop
metas.note:
Reverse L-shaped poletops are common in British Columbia and Québec - especially on the Gaspé-peninsula.

Note: The insulators and the colour of the wood are different in the two provinces.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Eastern Canada  - A frame pole
metas.note:
If you see an A-frame pole, New Brunswick is the most likely option followed by Newfoundland & Labrador, Québec and Ontario.

Note: While these poles are generally rare in Canada, they can occasionally show up in any part of the country. Look for other clues first!
metas.footer: meta from: original find based on "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: Eastern Canada  - Eastern white pine
metas.note:
The Eastern white pine (Pinus strobus) can be recognised by its oval crown, long needles and horizontal, tiered branches. It is useful for getting the Eastern half of the country in ultra-rural rounds.

Tip: If you see it in very large quantities, you are probably further South within its range. (Eg: somewhere close to the Great Lakes, the New England border or Southern Nova Scotia).
metas.footer: meta from: original research

metas.name: Eastern Canada  - Isolated UFO insulator
metas.note:
Isolated stubby ribbed insulators (UFO shape) can be found in Ontario, Québec and Newfoundland & Labrador.

Note: Some regions have more of them, such as the extreme Southwest in Ontario or the far East of Québec.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Eastern Canada  - Lighter poles
metas.note: Utility poles in Eastern Canada (The Maritimes and Québec - especially the East) are made of a lighter coloured wood and have more visible knots on them.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: Eastern Canada  - Maple trees
metas.note:
Canada is home to 10 native maple species, including the iconic Sugar Maple (Acer saccharum) and the Red Maple (Acer rubrum). These trees can be recognised by their large round crowns and lobed leaves - just like the one on the Canadian flag. On fall coverage, their brilliant orange-red foliage can be seen from far away. You can find a lot of these trees in the St. Lawrence Lowlands and the Maritimes.

Note: Maples are useful for excluding the Northern parts of Ontario and Québec, as well as NL.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Eastern Canada  - Tiny hanging lamp
metas.note:
An old-timey looking lamp hanging from a very short, triangle shaped arm is unique to the Maritime Provinces. It is by far the most common in Nova Scotia.

Note: While I haven't seen this design on Newfoundland Island, Labrador seems to like it a lot. More research needs to be done on PEI.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: Manitoba  - Gravel ditch
metas.note: A thick strip of light coloured gravel on the sides of the road is a good clue for Manitoba. On many roads white outer lines are entirely replaced by gravel ditches.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: Manitoba  - Hanging insulator poletop
metas.note:
Trident poletops with 2 hanging insulators are pretty much unique to Manitoba. They exist with or without a secondary crossbar.

Note: This poletop is way more common on the Southern plains of Manitoba than further North.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: Manitoba  - Insulator patterns
metas.note:
Manitoba's wooden poles can have the same 2+1 arrangement as Saskatchewan's, but they will not alternate consistently. It is possible to find poles with different insulator patterns standing right next to each other.

Note: Manny's crossbars are also shorter and the insulators are often smaller or darker than Sask's.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: Manitoba  - Keyhole sticker
metas.note: Even though rural pole stickers are quite unreliable on the Prairies, Manitoba's poles often have a distinct metal sticker shaped like a "keyhole". (A circle with a trapezoid underneath).
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: Manitoba  - Long supported lamp arm
metas.note:
An excessively long, supported lamp arm will most likely put you in Manitoba.

Note: Most of Manitoba's lamp arms will be the standard Canadian style though.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: Manitoba  - October snow
metas.note: East of Winnipeg, nearby the border with Ontario 2 roads with patchy snow coverage can be found (MB 307 and the Eastern part of Hwy 44). The images were taken in October (copyright is 2019) with a Gen 3 camera, so there is a distinct Autumnal feel to them. The landscape is hilly and forested.
metas.footer: meta from: original find

metas.name: Manitoba  - Side wire attachment
metas.note: Wires attached to the side of the pole are more common in Manitoba than in the other Prairies provinces.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: Manitoba  - Sign clasp
metas.note: Rural towns in Manitoba still use metal sign clasps specific to the province.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: Manitoba  - Trident poletop
metas.note:
Manitoba's most iconic poletop is a long trident with long insulators, often with a secondary crossbar underneath.

Note: It also exists with alternative insulator types - what matters is the long trident shape.
metas.footer: meta from: original find, based on "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: Manitoba  - Typical landscape
metas.note: The typical Manitoban landscape features a mix of gently rolling hills and flat agricultural fields with patches of aspen parks in between. The open Prairie-like parts are in the South / Southwest, then you see a gradual transition into the boreal pine forest as you move Northeast.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: New Brunswick  - 1 bolt pole
metas.note: Many insulators in New Brunswick are fixed with only 1 bolt to the pole. The rest of Canada uses 2.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: New Brunswick  - Bollards
metas.note:
New Brunswick has a variety of rectangular bollards, usually found at guardrail-endings. Most common colours: green, pink and yellow (famously on the Trans-Canada Highway).

Note: Blocky-looking wooden bollards with a red or green reflector are also possible to get.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: New Brunswick  - Double insulator pole
metas.note:
Poles with two insulators on top are more common in New Brunswick than in any other province.

Note: Newfoundland and Labrador seems to have a lot of these poles too.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: New Brunswick  - Forested hills
metas.note: The typical New Brunswick landscape consists of lush rolling hills covered in evergreens, such as pines and spruces.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: New Brunswick  - Generic guardrail
metas.note: New Brunswick uses pretty generic looking guardrails. This is useful for differentiating between NB and the other Maritimes (especially NS and NL) that use more unique guardrail types.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: New Brunswick  - Green sticker
metas.note:
Directional signs and poles at larger intersections in New Brunswick often have a green sticker with white lettering on the signpost.

Note: Many of these green stickers have "New Brunswick" written on the top alongside a logo, but you need to go close to be able to read it.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: New Brunswick  - Language regions
metas.note: You can subdivide New Brunswick by how much French language you can see around. The Northern counties and the East coast are Acadian territory where most text will be bilingual (or French only). In the Central and Southern counties the usage of French will be limited to street signs and official buildings.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: New Brunswick  - Long straight lamp
metas.note:
New Brunswick lamps can be recognised by their length and straightness. They usually feature square lamps with a blue photocell on top.

Note: Lamp arms in Nova Scotia are shorter and more curved.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: New Brunswick  - No roadlines coverage
metas.note: New Brunswick has a lot of coverage on rural asphalt roads without any roadlines.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: New Brunswick  - Yellow pole sticker
metas.note: Yellow horizontal pole stickers with black numbers are common in New Brunswick. There can be one or more on the same utility pole.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: New Brunswick / Nova Scotia  - Curved sign border
metas.note:
Rural road signs with a white, curved border can be found in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick.

Note: This is a pretty standard design for directional signs in all of Canada, so make sure it says a road name to narrow it down to NS or NB!
metas.footer: meta from: original find based on "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: New Brunswick / Nova Scotia  - Stoplight styles
metas.note:
Nova Scotia and New Brunswick use similar stoplight designs, but NS is more likely to use solid yellow ones, while NB has more solid black ones, or yellow ones with a black middle part.

Note: The city of Amherst (NS) close to the border with NB uses solid black stoplights.
metas.footer: meta from: original find

metas.name: Newfoundland  - Burin dryness
metas.note:
The Burin Peninsula in the far South of Newfoundland has a distinctly dry and barren landscape.

Note: The general South of Newfoundland tends to be dryer and have fewer trees than the rest of it.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: Newfoundland  - Eastern insulator
metas.note:
Insulators whose top rib is larger than the bottom one are the most common on the Eastern parts of Newfoundland. The Avalon Peninsula seems to love them a lot.

Note: There is another insulator type on the island with 2 equally small ribs and a larger top one. This is not specific to the East!
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: Newfoundland  - Eastern poletop
metas.note:
A poletop with 2 horizontal insulators pointing in opposite directions and one vertical insulator on top is commonly found on the Eastern part of Newfoundland.

Note: If you see this poletop in a cloudy October landscape with a 2019 copyright you are on road NL-230. On Gen 4 it's probably the NL-10 South of St. John's, but there might be more around.
metas.footer: meta from: original find

metas.name: Newfoundland  - Exposed rock
metas.note: Just like in Ontario, it is common to find exposed rock lining the road in Newfoundland.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: Newfoundland  - Southwestern mountains
metas.note: The Southwestern edge of Newfoundland has a very distinct looking green mountain range visible from the Trans-Canada Highway.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: Newfoundland & Labrador  - Bollards
metas.note:
Regular bollards are not too common in Newfoundland and Labrador, but you can sometimes find a rustic-looking wooden bollard at the end of the guardrails, as well as various interesting snowpoles.

Note: It is relatively common to see snowpoles on the side of residential driveways in NL.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage (and some original research)

metas.name: Newfoundland & Labrador  - Double crossbar poletop
metas.note:
One of Newfoundland & Labrador's most common poletops is a trident poletop with double crossbars and thick insulators.

Note: The shape of the insulators can vary.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: Newfoundland & Labrador  - Extra short lamp
metas.note:
Lamps with extra short arms are a unique feature of Newfoundland and Labrador.

Note: The rest of their lamps are similar to the old, curved lamps of Nova Scotia.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: Newfoundland & Labrador  - Long trident poletop
metas.note:
The second most common poletop in Newfoundland and Labrador is a trident poletop with a low crossbar and long insulators.

Note: Manitoba's trident poletop looks similar, but that one has skinnier insulators and a second crossbar below the main one. (Not to mention the landscape couldn't be more different.)
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: Newfoundland & Labrador  - Metal plate
metas.note: A simple horizontal metal plate is hiding in plain sight on the utility poles of Newfoundland and Labrador.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: Newfoundland & Labrador  - Provincial routes
metas.note:
Regular provincial routes in Newfoundland and Labrador are signed as a black number inside a white rectangle. They are organised regionally.

Useful to know:

  • 2 digit routes starting with a 2 are on the Avalon Peninsula
  • the 500s are in Labrador
metas.footer: meta and map from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: Newfoundland & Labrador  - Short trident poletop
metas.note: The iconic long trident poletop of Newfoundland and Labrador has a very common variant with shorter vertical bars. The isulators can vary (usually stubby with 3 ribs or long with many ribs).
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: Newfoundland & Labrador  - Wooden signpost
metas.note:
Within Atlantic Canada only Newfoundland and Labrador uses thick wooden signposts consistently.

Note: Nova Scotia has a mix of wooden and metal posts, while the rest of the Maritimes mostly uses square metal posts with small holes.
metas.footer: meta from: original find

metas.name: Northwest Territories  - Canadian Shield
metas.note:
If you see exposed rocks by the road in the far Northwest, you are just North of the Great Slave Lake around Yellowknife (Roads NT-3 and 4).

Note: This is the Westernmost edge of the Canadian Shield.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: Northwest Territories  - Other bollards
metas.note:
The Northwest Territories has a few bollards not discussed on the Plonkit guide, even though many of them are more common than the Alberta-style variant. The two main types:

  • a hollow metal stick with a white or yellow rectangular part bolted on top
  • a square-shaped wooden bollard painted white

The exact designs are often specific to a certain road. (More about that on the Rural Roads map.)
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: Northwest Territories  - Southern vibes
metas.note:
Southern Northwest Territories has a distinct vibe to it, featuring similar tall and skinny looking pines to Yukon but on a way flatter landscape.

Note: The whole Southern coverage is extremely sunny, except for some roads North and South of the Great Slave Lake.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: Northwest Territories  - Unpaved roads
metas.note:
The are only 3 unpaved roads in the Northwest Territories with official coverage:

  • the Dempster Highway (NT-8) to Inuvik
  • the Liard Highway (NT-7)
  • the MacKenzie Highway (NT-1) from a little South of Fort Simpson to a little West of the intersection with the NT-3
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: Northwest Territories  - White highway post
metas.note: Just like Yukon, the Northwest Territories also use thick white wooden highway signposts.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: Nova Scotia  - Bilingualism
metas.note: A little more than 10% of the inhabitants of Nova Scotia are bilingual. The most prominent Francophone areas are found on the Southern coast (centered around Yarmouth), the West coast of Cape Breton Island (Chéticamp, Margaree Harbour) and Southern Cape Breton Island (Isle Madame and surroundings). In these areas bilingual signs and the colours of the Acadian flag are a common sight.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: https://www.plonkit.net/.

metas.name: Nova Scotia  - Green signback
metas.note: Green signbacks aren't exclusive to British Columbia and PEI: they are fairly common in Nova Scotia too. Here you will often find them supported by thick wooden or metal cross beams.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: Nova Scotia  - Guardrail sticks
metas.note: Nova Scotia likes to place colourful snowpoles at the end of her guardrails. The most common style is yellow with a red reflector, but there are lots of possible variations.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: Nova Scotia  - Hilly landscape
metas.note: Nova Scotia is generally hilly and has the thick vegetation typical of Eastern Canada. The highest elevation areas can be found on the Cape Breton Island, followed by the Cobequid Mountains on the mainland part.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: Nova Scotia  - Isolated exit number
metas.note:
While highway signage in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick looks quite similar, only NS uses isolated exit numbers above the sign.

Note: The shape of the extra piece is useful, even when you view it from behind!
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: Nova Scotia  - Pokey guardrail
metas.note:
In Nova Scotia the wooden block that connects to the metal part of the guardrail is usually long enough to poke out under the guardrail. This is not the case in New Brunswick.

Note: The yellow reflectors are also more typical for Nova Scotia than for NB.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: Nova Scotia  - Québec style poletop
metas.note:
It is fairly common to see Québec-style poletops in Nova Scotia, especially in the larger towns.

Note: The shape of the lamp attached will be different in the two provinces.
metas.footer: meta from: original find

metas.name: Nova Scotia  - Reflector guardrail
metas.note: Another common guardrail type in Nova Scotia is one without the extra woodblock. The yellow reflector tapes are still present on each leg.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: Nova Scotia  - Short crossbeam poletop
metas.note:
The main poletop in Nova Scotia has a noticeably short and low crossbeam.

Note: The middle insulator is perpendicular to the wires.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: Nova Scotia  - Short curved lamp
metas.note:
Lamps in Nova Scotia tend to have short, curved arms. There are 3 types of common lamp heads:

  • bulky and round (more on older coverage)
  • the "classic" square shaped
  • long and flat (more on newer coverage)
metas.footer: meta from: original find based on "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: Nova Scotia  - Wire sticker
metas.note:
In Nova Scotia it is common to see red stickers wrapped around, or hanging from wires. The stickers can sometimes also show up in New Brunswick.

Note: The wire flags of Ontario and Québec can look very similar, but there you are more likely to see multiple stickers next to one another. Also, Nova Scotia doesn't use circle stickers. Look for other clues first!
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: Ontario  - 3 tall ribbed insulators
metas.note:
Tall ribbed insulators are most common Ontario, followed by BC and NL. Crossarm poles with 3 tall ribbed insulators however are only found in Ontario.

Note: The 3 insulators can be upright or tilted.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Ontario  - Bilingualism
metas.note:
English-French bilingualism within Ontario is typically found in the East. Main areas include Greater Sudbury, the Ottawa area close to the Québec border and around Kapuskasing in the Northeast.

Note: The region East of Sudbury has an excessive amount of bilingual signage.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Ontario  - Blue cap guardrail
metas.note:
In some areas of Ontario, the standard wire guardrails have been replaced with a wire guardrail on steel posts with a blue cap on top.

Note: Highway 144 is a notable example, but it appears on many Northern highways on Gen 4.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Ontario  - Colourful markings
metas.note: In Ontario it is common to see one or more colourful circles on the utility poles. Usually, they are red, blue or white, but I have also seen black and brown ones.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Ontario  - County road sign
metas.note:
Southern Ontario uses a specific street sign design that includes the county name under the road name. They can also show numbers and direction arrows.

Note: These signs are most common in the extreme Southwest, but can also be found further East.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Ontario  - Gen 3 snow
metas.note:
While most of the sunny Gen 3 snow coverage in Northwestern Ontario has been overwritten, there are still a few roads left where you can see it.

Full snow coverage:

  • between Eagle River and Sioux Lookout
  • ON 594 West of Dryden

Patchy, melting snow:

  • ON 622 around the Turtle River Provincial Park
  • ON 502 and ON 594 very close to Dryden
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage + original find.

metas.name: Ontario  - Green electrical box
metas.note: This specific design of the green electrical box with the yellow numbers is common in residential areas throughout Ontario. Many of them also have a danger sticker or a circle sticker on it, although the numbers are enough to identify the design.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Ontario  - GTA octo lamp
metas.note:
In the Greater Toronto Area a unique lamp can be found in large quantities. Although its top is usually very distinct, what makes it count as a meta is its octagonal shape and spotted grey colour.

Note: The post exists with more generic lamp heads too.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Ontario  - Intersection pole ring
metas.note: In rural intersections in Southern Ontario you can sometimes encouter these short wooden poles with a ring on them. The ring can be white, yellow, orange or red and can appear on other signposts too. There are a few exception locations in Québec.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Ontario  - Knotty fence
metas.note:
Wooden fences in Ontario are usually quite knotty and uneven. Prairie fences are smoother with a flat top.

Note: These fences are typically found in agricultural areas (St. Lawrence Lowlands and the Clay Belt).
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Ontario  - Larger top lamp
metas.note:
Ontario's traffic lights are unique, because the top lamp is larger than the bottom two. This is only true for 3-lamp setups, 4-lamp traffic lights are usually uniform.

Note: Rarely, you can find traffic lights without this feature in Ontario, especially in downtown Toronto.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Ontario  - LCBO Stores
metas.note: The LCBO (Liquor Control Board of Ontario) is a chain of government-owned liquor stores that only operates in Ontario. Around the big Southern cities you can find large LCBO stores with spacious parking lots, while in the rural Northern towns small convenience store locations are more common.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Ontario  - Longer crossarm
metas.note:
With a bit of training you might notice that Ontario uses a longer crossarm on its generic Canadian poles that most other provinces. In addition, the middle insulator will be parallel to the wire.

Note: Long crossarms can also be seen in Saskatchewan.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Ontario  - Metal guardrail
metas.note: Besides wire guardrails, Ontario also uses metal guardrails with metal or wooden supports. Metal supports are common on large freeways, while the wooden ones are found on smaller highways.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Ontario  - Northern red hydrants
metas.note:
Although most of Ontario uses yellow body fire hydrants, a few regional exceptions exist where the dominant hydrant colour is red.

Notable areas in Central and Northern Ontario:

  • Sault Ste Marie
  • a few towns around Lac Seul (Sioux Lookout, Dryden)
  • Nipigon
  • Fort Frances
  • a few smaller towns in the Clay Belt (Englehart, Earlton)

...and some other very tiny exceptions.

Note: Fire hydrants in the North tend to have a snow pole attached.
metas.footer: meta source: original find

metas.name: Ontario  - Number stickers
metas.note:
Utility poles in Ontario can have a variety of yellow number stickers on them. Variants include a vertical sticker with 5-6 numbers, a horizontal version, and a much larger type with inverted colours.

Note: Some of the smaller yellow plates are fixed to the pole using 2 black rings.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Ontario  - Paired boxes
metas.note: A green electrical box paired up with a small brown one is a common sight in the suburbs of far Southern Ontario.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Ontario  - Railway poletop
metas.note: Nearby railway tracks in Ontario poles with a large number of small insulators can be present. These poletops can have a lot of extra crossarms.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Ontario  - Rectangular signpost
metas.note:
The most common signpost in (semi) urban Ontario is a rectangular metal pole with small holes on it. Other provinces use solid or round signposts more often.

Note: In rural areas thick wooden signposts are even more common.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Ontario  - Rural address colours
metas.note:
About 80% of rural adress signs in Ontario are green. Exceptions exist in the far West and far East of the province, where they are often blue.

Note: Within Canada, green rural address signs are more common West of Ontario and blue ones are more common East of it.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Ontario  - Rural street sign
metas.note:
Rural street signs in Ontario are usually green, with white block letters in a specific font / style. The roads are often named "concession", "line" or "sideroad", especially on the far Southern grid.

Note: Many large cities (Toronto, Ottawa, Kitchener, Niagara Falls) use blue street signs instead.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Ontario  - Silver numbers
metas.note:
Large silver numbers bolted on the utility poles are common in Ontario. They can be arranged vertically, diagonally or horizontally and usually you can also see the bolts holding them up.

Note: In reality, you will often find a mix of different markings on the pole.
metas.footer: meta from: original find.

metas.name: Ontario  - Small pole plate
metas.note: A very small, vertical pole plate made of metal can be found on utility poles accross Ontario.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: Ontario  - Southern architecture
metas.note:
Suburbs in Southern Ontario have a very distinct architectural style.

A few common features to look for:

  • the main building material is red brick
  • square roof vents or chimney shaped vents
  • trapezoid accent bricks
  • oval shaped gable windows
  • driveways being cut by sidewalks.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Ontario  - Southern red hydrants
metas.note:
While most fire hydrants in Ontario are yellow, a few regional exceptions exist. In the South, the regions of Hamilton, Halton, Peel and some towns in Niagara consistently use red body hydrants.

Note: For some reason Grimsby, Lincoln and St. Catharines stick with yellow.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Ontario  - Tilted attachment
metas.note:
A tilted attachment piece under the insulator is unique for Ontario. It can appear both on single insulator poles and the classic V-shape Ontario poletops, under the middle insulator. The insulators themselves are usually ribbed and sit parallel to the wire.

Note: V-poletops in BC don't have this attachment.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Ontario  - V-shaped sewer cover
metas.note: The most prevalent sewer cover type in Ontario has a V-shape design. This is almost completely unique to Ontario.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Ontario  - Wooden signpost
metas.note: In rural areas, Ontario likes to use thick, unpainted wooden signposts for information signs and traffic signs. Québec prefers metal.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Ontario  - Yellow fire hydrants
metas.note:
Most of Ontario uses yellow-body fire hydrants. The nozzle and top colours vary from town to town and can be used for more specific guesses. (For more hydrant tips see: "Comprehensive Canada - Cities").

Note: There are a few notable sub-regions in Ontario with red fire hydrants.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Ontario / British Columbia  - Secondary crossarm
metas.note:
Secondary crossarms on utility poles are typical in Ontario and British Columbia. To differentiate between the two provinces, you can check the following:

  • Ontario usually has a tilted attachment under the middle insulator
  • Ontario commonly uses a V-shape poletop or 3 ribbed insulators, while BC prefers white mushrooms
  • secondary crossarms in BC are usually longer.

Note: In the Prairies you will only see large secondary crossarm poles with downward facing insulators. The Maritimes don't use secondary crossarms.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Ontario / British Columbia  - Tilted insulators
metas.note:
Poletops with 3 tilted insulators are commonly found in British Columbia and Ontario.

Tips to differentiate:

  • tall, ribbed insulators are always Ontario
  • BC prefers "mushrooms" or UFO-shaped insulators
  • tilted insulators in a 2+1 pattern are BC only.

Note: I have seen tilted insulator poletops in Nova Scotia too. Look at the colour of the wood to rule it out!
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Ontario / Manitoba  - Mini insulators
metas.note:
Insulators that are visibly smaller than the standard can be found in Ontario and Manitoba. They can appear on single insulator poles or full crossarm poletops.

Note: Mini insulators can sometimes appear in Saskatchewan and rarely in Alberta too.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Ontario / Québec  - Corn production
metas.note:
Most of Canada's corn production happens in Southern Ontario and Québec, in the St. Lawrence Lowlands.

Note: Wheat and canola are more common in the Clay Belt and the Prairies.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Ontario / Québec  - Curve ahead signs
metas.note:
You can tell Ontario and Québec apart by their curve ahead signs: the ones in Ontario curve noticeably less than the ones in Québec.

Note: The post material will also be different.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: Ontario / Québec  - Farms
metas.note:
The farms on the St. Lawrence Lowlands have a very unique architectural style. The most distinct are the white top circular grain silos and the roof shape of the stables.

The following elements are more typical for Ontario (and extreme SW Québec) than Québec:

  • fancy vents and roof decorations
  • multiple large grain silos
  • horses
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Ontario / Québec  - Wire flags
metas.note: Orange flags and circles are quite common to find on wires near the pole in Ontario and Québec. The circles can be yellow too.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Prairies  - Orange-red wire marker
metas.note:
Orange-red underground wire markers can be found in all three Prairie Provinces. They are the most consistent in Alberta.

Note: In Saskatchewan, yellow markers are also common.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Prairies  - Smooth fence
metas.note: Wooden fences on the Prairies tend to be smooth, with a flat top. (Fences in Ontario usually have knots and are of worse quality).
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Prince Edward Island  - Bilingual street sign
metas.note: Bilingualism on Prince Edward Island is regional: it is more present in the West, especially in the Evangeline region (West of Summerside). Despite this, most street signs will be bilingual in the province, while the STOP signs will be in English only.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: Prince Edward Island  - Hilly areas
metas.note:
While most of Prince Edward Island is quite flat, you can find rolling hills in a few notable areas:

  1. West of Charlottetown
  2. Just South of Montague
  3. In the Far Northeast, North of Souris
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: Prince Edward Island  - Ribbed insulator poletops
metas.note: A distinct poletop with 3 long thin ribbed insulators can be found on Prince Edward Island. A variant of this poletop with 2 angled up brackets, just like an Ontario poletop is specific to the region North of Montague.
metas.footer: meta from: original find based on "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: Prince Edward Island  - Standard pole
metas.note:
The most dominant pole on Prince Edward Island is similar to the Nova Scotia pole (insulators perpendicular to the wire, crossbar not as high up as in NB), but it has a slightly longer crossbar.

Note: The lamps can be both NB and NS style.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: Québec  - Appalachian vibes
metas.note:
South of the St. Lawrence River in Québec a rolling landscape can be seen with a mix of pines (mostly Eastern White pine) and broadleaf trees. This area is part of the Appalachian Mountains so it can look a lot like the neighbouring states of the US (Maine, Vermont or New Hampshire).

Note: The elevation gets much higher as you get to the Gaspé peninsula in the East.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Québec  - Cement block
metas.note: In Québec, wires leading to the ground often feed into a covered cement block at the base of the pole.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Québec  - Curved lamp
metas.note:
Lamps in Québec curve more than in other provinces.

Note: They are longer than the curved lamps found in the Maritimes.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: Québec  - Double signpost
metas.note: In Québec signs are often held up by 2 metal signposts.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Québec  - Gaspé lamp
metas.note: S-curve lamps are typically found on the Gaspé Peninsula. Many of them have an extra support bar below.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Québec  - Guardrail endings
metas.note:
In Québec, guardrails can end in 2 ways:

  • flat, with black and yellow stripes
  • in a simple hoop.

In both cases you will see a snow pole-like bollard at the end of the guardrail.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Québec  - Horizontal stoplight
metas.note: Québec uses horizontal stoplights. Most of them are fully black, but yellow outlines are also common.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Québec  - Laurentides
metas.note:
North of the St. Lawrence River you can see the Laurentian Mountain Range. The densely forested mountains get taller the further East you go with some impressive heights just North of Québec City.

Note: The Laurentides are part of the Canadian Shield, so exposed rocks lining the road in a green montainous environment is a good clue for the area. You won't get mountains of this size in Ontario.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Québec  - Metal signpost
metas.note:
In comparison to other provinces, Québec uses a lot of metal signposts. They usually have little holes on them.

Note: This comes in handy for Ontario - Québec 50/50s as Ontario prefers thick wooden posts in rural areas.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Québec  - Snowmobile sign
metas.note: Designated snowmobile trails are common in Québec, especially on the Northern roads. They are indicated by yellow diamond signs with the pictogram of a snowmobile, or more rarely also a quad bike.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Québec  - Southwestern cross
metas.note: Cross signbacks are a good clue for Southwestern Québec. (Usually on the plains South of Montréal).
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Québec  - Unique lamp arm
metas.note: Double lamp arms with 2 vertical bars in between are unique to Québec.
metas.footer: Meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Québec / New Brunswick  - T pole
metas.note:
On generic poletops, the horizontal crossbar is higher up in Québec and New Brunswick than in the other Canadian provinces. (The pole looks more like a "T" than a "t".)

Note: Middle insulators in Québec are perpendicular to the wire, in NB they are parallel.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Québec / Nova Scotia  - Perpendicular insulator
metas.note:
In Québec, Nova Scotia and on Prince Edward Island middle insulators (or standalone insulators) will be perpendicular to the wire.

Note: Parallel is the Canadian standard.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: Saskatchewan  - "Alberta" bollards
metas.note:
Bollards are a rare sight in Sask due to the straighness of their roads, but beware: on major roads you can sometimes see "Alberta-style" bollards. Manitoba-style ones are also possible, but these are even rarer.

Note: Most of Sask's bollards are found in highway intersections close to one of the largest cities. If you see a bollard on a random rural road you are probably somewhere else.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: Saskatchewan  - Blank metal strip
metas.note:
Rural pole stickers in Saskatchewan can be quite random, but a completely blank silver metal strip is commonly seen.

Note: Alberta has a similar sticker, but it is more likely to feature numbers. Use with caution.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Saskatchewan  - Extreme flatness
metas.note:
Saskatchewan is a very flat province - even by Prairies standards.

Note: Do no forget about the barren Cypress Hills of the Far Southwest!
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Saskatchewan  - Gas pipeline marker
metas.note:
Upon leaving rural towns in Sask it is very common to see high pressure natural gas pipelines marked by a warning sign unique to the province. The sign can be white or red, with an oval shape on top saying "DANGER".

Note: It can be found in rolled up form too, like the underground wire markers.
metas.footer: meta from: original research

metas.name: Saskatchewan  - Green lamp
metas.note:
Isolated lamps in Saskatchewan are often green.

Note: They are commonly seen in suburbs and small towns.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: Saskatchewan  - Guardrail loop
metas.note: Guardrails are quite rare in Saskatchewan, but when you do see them they end in an open loop and lack the holes seen on Alberta guardrails.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: Saskatchewan  - Lamp support
metas.note: Lamps in Saskatchewan are often curved and have a support bar underneath. (About 60% of their lamps are like this.)
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: Saskatchewan  - Long crossarm pole
metas.note:
If you can't find typical 2+1 alternating insulator poletops in Sask, you can still rely on the excessive lenght of the crossbar to identify the province.

Note: Ontario also likes long crossarms.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Saskatchewan  - Lower insulator
metas.note: In Saskatchewan, you can sometimes find insulators that are mounted lower than the generic Canadian ones. Not every insulator will be like this, but it is a unique feature of Sask.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Saskatchewan  - Northern vegetation
metas.note: The further North you go in Saskatchewan, the more vegetation you will see. The absolute flatness of the Prairies gradually gives way to boreal forests on slightly hillier terrain.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Saskatchewan  - Rare poletops
metas.note:
Northern Saskatchewan is home to a wide range of intriguing poletops.

Note: The "missing insulator pole" in Alberta is missing its insulator on the bottom bar, otherwise it is similar to the one in the example.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Saskatchewan  - Rural road quality
metas.note: Rural roads in Saskatchewan tend to be thinner and in a worse condition than in Alberta (or Manitoba). Roads that have been patched up a few times are a common sight here.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage.

metas.name: Saskatchewan  - Rural street sign
metas.note:
Rural street signs in Saskatchewan are usually green with white letters. Be careful: calling roads "range road" or "township road" aren't exclusive to Alberta - they are also common here!

Note: Most of Alberta's rural street signs are blue.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: Saskatchewan  - White signpost
metas.note:
White-painted wooden signposts are commonly found in Saskatchewan.

Note: Yukon and NWT often use white wooden signposts for their highway signs, but not for their small traffic signs.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: Saskatchewan  - Yellow wire marker
metas.note:
While orange/red underground wire markers are the standard within the Prairies, Saskatchewan also uses yellow markers. These are unique within the Prairies.

Note: Yellow markers are also typical in Ontario, Québec and BC.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: Saskatchewan / Manitoba  - Weird guardrails
metas.note:
While guardrails in general are quite rare in the Prairies, you can sometimes come accross a few alternative guardrails in Saskatchewan and Manitoba.

  • in Sask, this means either a wire guardrail with 2 wires close together or a short square wooden guardrail
  • in Manny, it's usually a wire guardrail with 3 wires

Note: Alberta prefers "normal" guardrails.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage + original research

metas.name: Yukon  - Complicated crossbeam
metas.note: Utility poles in Yukon can have rather complicated secondary crossbeams. They can be assymmetrical or twisted and they usually have a number of extra insulators on them.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: Yukon  - Orange tint pole
metas.note: Most utility poles in Yukon are generic T-poles with a distinct orange tint.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: Yukon  - Pink fireweed
metas.note:
Fireweed (Chamerion angustifolium) is Yukon's floral emblem. While it can be found all over the province, you can only see the bright pink flowers bloom on the Gen 2 July coverage. This means 2 main areas in the far South:

  • on Route 3 (Haines Road) between the Dezadeash Lake and the BC border
  • the roads Southeast of Whitehorse (the area around Tagish)
  • on Route 1 (Alaska Highway) around Upper Liard and also West of it

Note: On Gen 4 you will see the leaves and stems of the plant changing into dark reddish Autumn colours. Autumn fireweed has a larger range.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage + original research

metas.name: Yukon  - September 2022
metas.note:
The newer Gen 4 coverage in Yukon was captured in September (©2022). It is easy to recognise from the extremely vibrant yellow-orange Autumn colours.

Note: Yukon has only Gen 2 and Gen 4.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: Yukon  - Snowpoles
metas.note:
Instead of bollards, Yukon prefers to use a variety of thin snowpoles. Most common designs: thick stripes of 2 colours, or one base colour + a different top. The snowpoles come in handy in border 50/50-s with BC or NWT which use their own bollards.

Note: The exact pattern of colours is often specific to a certain road. (More on that in the Rural Roads map.)
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: Yukon  - Treeless mountains
metas.note: Mountains in Yukon are mostly treeless and brownish of colour. They are usually seen in the distance.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: Yukon  - Unpaved roads
metas.note:
Knowing which roads are unpaved is useful in Yukon. The largest cluster is in the East, on the Route 4 (Robert Campbell Highway) between Faro and Tuchitua and its offroads including Route 6.

Secondly, Routes 5 (Dempster Higway) and 9 (Top of the World Highway) in the far North are unpaved too.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage + original research

metas.name: Yukon  - White highway post
metas.note:
Highway signposts in Yukon are usually made of thick white-painted wood.

Note: NWT also uses white signposts. BC prefers them unpainted.
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage

metas.name: Yukon / British Columbia  - Cloudy border
metas.note:
Gen 2 coverage with very gloomy, cloudy weather can be found on both sides of the BC - Yukon border.

Note: The pictures were taken in July so you can sometimes see pink fireweed around. (©2019)
metas.footer: meta from: "A Comprehensive Canada" by Davis Savage
